title: Splash to Save
bodyHtml:
Ende is a Pahoturi River language spoken by 600 to 1,000 people in Western Province, Papua New Guinea. Ende speakers are often multilingual due to marriages with speakers of other languages (e.g., Taeme and Kawam). However, in this problem we focus only on Ende. The first part of an Ende story is given below, with the English translation of each sentence directly below the Ende.1

(1) Ankom a tärko ubi eragwaeya ddobae ai abal nag dagwaeya.
Ant and Small Fish, they were really very good friends.

(2) Ankom obo ma me daeya llo toko me.
Ant was in his house on top of a tree.

(3) Tärko walle me daeya ddob kollba nagnag oba peyang.
Small Fish was in the river with some fish friends.

(4) Ttongo ag me däbe ttängäm a säresäremang gogon.
One morning that place was about to rain.

(5) Yäbäd de ddapall käkan da dakonewän.
Clouds covered the sun.

(6) Malla wätali gogon, wel ulle da gongkamän.
It wasn't long before a big wind began.

1. Pronunciation notes:

  • ä is a vowel similar to the first syllable of the English word about.
  • tt is similar to ch in English (as in church), except that tt is retroflex, meaning that it is pronounced with the tip of the tongue facing the back of the mouth.
  • dd is similar to the first and last sounds of the English word judge, except that dd is retroflex.
  • ll is similar to English r (as in read).

The rest of the story

The English translation for the rest of the story is presented below. The Ende sentences follow, in scrambled order.

(7) It blew down and broke the tree.

(8) The wind tore Ant's house and threw Ant into the river.

(9) When Small Fish saw, he moved closer to him.

(10) But some big fish were trying to kill him.

(11) A catfish was about to swallow him.

(12) Small Fish quickly splashed with his tail, and with water threw Ant on top of the grass, and he was saved.

(A) Bunkuttang a mäse ngänygäny e dängkamän.

(B) Tärko da mängalae källa gokätaemän a ine peyang ankom bom towall toko we daspunän a ttam gogän.

(C) Ankom bo ma de wel a dapisamän a ankom bom daspunän walle we.

(D) Be ddob kollba ulleulle da gäz e de ada däganeyo.

(E) Llo de duduaibnegnän a dattkaemnegnän.

(F) Tärko da angde ikop dägagän, obo dowae e guinggolän.

F2.

Please provide English translations for the following Ende words:

a. tärko

b. walle

c. daspunän

d. gongkamän

e. yäbäd

F3.

Please provide Ende translations for the following words:

a. Ant

b. and

c. tree

d. catfish

F4.

List all of the words from the following list that would appear in the Ende translation for "Ant got on top of his house." You should give at least one word.

tärko, kollba, llo, me, toko, towall, ulleulle, we, wel

hints.text: Start with the two characters. Sentences (1)-(3) tell you which Ende word names each of the two friends, and those names show up again in the scrambled sentences (A)-(F). Any scrambled sentence whose English translation does not mention a character should not begin with a character's name.

Match on three kinds of clue at once: repeated nouns you can pin down from (1)-(6), sentence length (a long English sentence needs a long Ende sentence), and the little grammatical words. Ende puts short markers right after the subject and right after the object of a clause, and it also distinguishes being at rest in a place from moving into a place with different little words after the place expression. Comparing sentence (2) with sentence (12) is the key to the last question.

Here is the little-word method on data that is not graded. In sentence (2) the verb is daeya, since the same form appears in (3), which is also a "was in ..." sentence. That leaves two short place expressions in (2), and both end in the same word me, matching the English "in his house" and "on top of a tree". So me is a location word meaning roughly "in, at", and the place noun stands in front of it. Now check what happens in sentence (12), where somebody is moved to a new place.

explanationHtml:
Step 1: find the two characters

Sentence (1) says "Ant and Small Fish, they were really very good friends" and begins Ankom a tärko .... Sentence (2) is about Ant and begins Ankom; sentence (3) is about Small Fish and begins Tärko. So ankom names Ant, tärko names Small Fish, and the little word a squeezed between them in (1) is "and". You will see a again joining two verbs in some of the scrambled sentences, exactly like English "and".

Step 2: mine sentences (2)-(6) for nouns

Sentence (2): Ankom obo ma me daeya llo toko me = "Ant was in his house on top of a tree." daeya is the "was" (it turns up again in (3), another "was in ..." sentence), obo is "his", and the two place expressions ma me and llo toko me must be "in his house" and "on top of a tree". Both end in me, so me is the location word "in / at", ma is "house", llo is "tree", and toko adds "on top".

Sentence (3): Tärko walle me daeya ddob kollba nagnag oba peyang = "Small Fish was in the river with some fish friends." Since daeya is "was" and me is "in", walle is "river"; ddob kollba is "fish" and peyang is "friends".

Sentence (5): Yäbäd de ddapall käkan da dakonewän = "Clouds covered the sun." Notice the two little markers: de after the first noun and da after the second. Everywhere in this story da (and sometimes a) follows the subject of a clause, while de and bom follow the object. So ddapall käkan is the subject "clouds" and yäbäd is the object, "the sun".

Sentence (6): Malla wätali gogon, wel ulle da gongkamän = "It wasn't long before a big wind began." wel with the subject marker da is "wind", ulle is "big", and the final verb gongkamän means "(it) began".

Step 3: match the scrambled sentences

Now go looking for those known words.

  • (E) Llo de duduaibnegnän a dattkaemnegnän. starts with llo "tree" plus the object marker de, then two verbs joined by a "and". English (7) "It blew down and broke the tree" is the only translation with two verbs joined by "and" acting on the tree.
  • (C) Ankom bo ma de wel a dapisamän a ankom bom daspunän walle we. contains "house" as an object (ma de), "wind" as a subject (wel a), Ant twice, and walle "river". That is English (8).
  • (F) Tärko da angde ikop dägagän, obo dowae e guinggolän. has Small Fish as subject and two clauses, matching (9) "When Small Fish saw, he moved closer to him."
  • (D) Be ddob kollba ulleulle da gäz e de ada däganeyo. has "fish" plus a doubled form of "big" (ulleulle, for plural "big fish"), which is (10).
  • (A) Bunkuttang a mäse ngänygäny e dängkamän. is the only short sentence left, and it starts with a brand-new noun followed by the subject marker a. English (11) introduces one brand-new animal, a catfish, so bunkuttang is "catfish".
  • (B) is by far the longest Ende sentence and (12) is by far the longest English sentence: it contains Small Fish as subject, Ant with the object marker bom, and towall toko we for "on top of the grass".

Step 4: the verb "threw"

Compare (C) ... ankom bom daspunän walle we "threw Ant into the river" with (B) ... ankom bom towall toko we daspunän "threw Ant on top of the grass". Both have Ant marked as object by bom and both share the verb daspunän, so daspunän is "(it) threw (it)".

Step 5: "in" versus "into" for the last question

Look at what follows the place words. In (2) the place expressions end in me, and nothing moves: Ant simply is in his house on top of a tree. In (C) and (B) the place expressions end in we, and something is thrown to a new place: walle we "into the river", towall toko we "onto the top of the grass". So me is "in / at" (no motion) and we is "into / onto" (motion). "Ant got on top of his house" describes motion to a new position, so the Ende version needs the "on top" word together with the motion marker, and none of the other listed words ("small fish", "fish", "tree", "grass", "big", "wind", and the no-motion location marker) belong in that sentence.
_reviewNotes: Answer keys taken verbatim from the official solution pages (F1: 7=E, 8=C, 9=F, 10=D, 11=A, 12=B; F2 a-e; F3 a-d; F4 = toko and we). The official solution gives no per-part point breakdown, so the 10 points were distributed evenly across the 15 short blanks (0.5 each) with the remaining 2.5 assigned to F4 - adjust if a rubric surfaces. The booklet prints two decorative clip-art images (an ant and a fish) on page 1; they carry no data and were omitted rather than cropped. F4 is printed as a 'circle all the words' task; here it is a single text blank whose key lists both words.
